z-m-16-01.title: Is it an expression that gives a prime number whatever number you put in for n?
z-m-16-01.topic: Prime numbers and composite numbers, values of expressions with letters
z-m-16-01.goal: Learn that being right many times does not guarantee 'always,' adjust how sure you are to fit the data, and find a counterexample yourself.
z-m-16-01.material: A friend in the math club said, "When n is an integer that is 0 or greater, like 0, 1, 2, ..., the value of n×n+n+41 (n times n plus n plus 41) is always a prime number!" A prime number is a number that is at least 2 and whose only divisors are 1 and itself, and a number that is at least 2 and is not prime is a composite number.
z-m-16-01.thinking.0: Telling apart the number of cases checked from 'all cases'
z-m-16-01.thinking.1: Revising how sure you are according to new data
z-m-16-01.prereq.0: The meaning of prime and composite numbers (a prime is a number that is at least 2 and whose only divisors are 1 and itself)
z-m-16-01.prereq.1: Putting a number in for the letter n to find the value of an expression (n×n is n squared)
z-m-16-01.prereq.2: Calculating by dividing numbers of up to four digits by smaller numbers in order
z-m-16-01.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time new data comes out, choose what is closest to what you think now.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of data, separate the 'n you have checked' from the 'n you have not checked yet.'
z-m-16-01.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what is needed to talk about 'all n,' not just the number you have checked so far.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.0.info: When you put in n=1, 2, 3, 4, 5, the values are 43, 47, 53, 61, 71. All five are prime numbers.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think now about your friend's claim?
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.0.after: Five checks are a clue that supports the claim. But there are endlessly many n, so to say 'always,' you need to test more or find a reason.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: All five were prime, so we can say it is prime for any n
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Being right five times is a clue, not a check of every n. What more is needed to talk about 'all n'?
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It looks plausible, but I want to test whether it holds for larger n too
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You accepted the clue, and also thought about the fact that there are many n you have not checked yet.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It was right only for small n, and for large n a composite number will surely come out
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: There is also no evidence yet that it fails for large n. Before checking, you cannot be sure either way.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: From five cases alone we can know nothing at all about this expression
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The fact that all five times were prime is also information. Decide how much to believe it.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.1.info: A computer program calculated all 40 values from n=0 to n=39, and every value was a prime number.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: How do you see your friend's claim now?
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.1.after: Even if all 40 are right, that is not a proof. It is suitable to call it a plausible guess.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: All 40 were prime, so now we can say 'always prime'
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: 40 is many, but there are still values of n greater than 40. Even if the number checked is large, you have not checked 'all n.'
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: From n=40 on, it is the turn for composite numbers to come out
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Having been right before does not make it the 'turn' to be wrong next. Is there a reason you see it that way?
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is a plausible guess, but we do not yet know whether it holds for all n
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: It kept the point that as checks pile up, belief grows, but 'all' needs a reason or a check of everything.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: We have checked 40, so we don't need to check n=41 and after
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The part you checked is not the whole. There is still a part left unchecked.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.2.info: If you put in n=40, you get 40×40+40+41=1681. But 41×41 is also 1681.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: What does this result tell you about your friend's claim?
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.2.after: 1681=41×41 is not a prime number. One example shows that 'always prime' does not hold.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The first 40 were all prime, so the calculation for n=40 must be wrong
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: If you doubt a calculation, you can calculate again. You must not throw away a new result only because earlier results are many.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: From now on, we must say that composite numbers come out for all n
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You over-generalized to the opposite side. Finding one case does not make all cases the opposite.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Only n=40 is an exception, so we can say it is prime for most n
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: 'Most' has not been checked yet either. You need to find out whether composite numbers also come out for n=41 and after.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: A composite number came out at n=40, so 'always prime' is false
z-m-16-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You knew that one example breaks 'always,' and accepted the new result as it is.
z-m-16-01.s.s1.reflect: How did your certainty change when the results came for up to n=5, up to 39, and then n=40? What is different between correct examples piling up and a single wrong example appearing?
z-m-16-01.s.s2.prompt: Find 2 different values of n, with n an integer from 0 to 100, for which the value of n×n+n+41 is not prime (is composite), and enter them.
z-m-16-01.s.s2.hint.0: Up to n=39 they were all prime. Calculate the values in order from the next n on.
z-m-16-01.s.s2.hint.1: If a value is large, check whether it is divisible by 2, 3, 5, 7, ... in that order.
z-m-16-01.s.s2.ok.c1: n is an integer from 0 to 100.
z-m-16-01.s.s2.fail.c1: n is not an integer from 0 to 100.
z-m-16-01.s.s2.fail.c2: For this n the value is prime. Look for another n.
z-m-16-01.s.s2.explain: For n=40 it is 1681=41×41, for n=41 it is 41×41+41+41=1763=41×43, and for n=44 it is 2021=43×47, so composite numbers come out. Even though 40 cases were right, the counterexample came right after.
z-m-16-01.s.s3.prompt: You want to tell your club friend this: "Even if it was prime for every n from 0 to 39, you must not say 'always prime.'" Write the reason, using at least one value of n you found above.
z-m-16-01.s.s3.hint.0: First write down one n you found above and the result of the calculation for it.
z-m-16-01.s.s3.hint.1: Point out which word ('always') in your friend's statement that result does not agree with.
z-m-16-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it clear that the value is not prime at the n you gave?
z-m-16-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does it include the point that 'I checked a lot' and 'I checked every case' are different?
z-m-16-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say that even one example breaks 'always'?
z-m-16-01.s.s3.model.0: For n=40, 1681=41×41, so it is not prime. Even if 40 values were prime, if just one such n comes out, 'always prime' becomes false.
z-m-16-01.s.s3.model.1: No matter how many you check, you have not checked every n. In fact at n=41 you get 41×43=1763, a composite number, so you must not say 'always.'
z-m-16-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: It contains both ideas: one counterexample, and 'the whole, not the count.'

z-m-16-02.title: When two buses next leave together for the first time
z-m-16-02.goal: Tell apart a value that holds in common from the value that holds 'for the first time,' design pairs of intervals yourself that fit the conditions, and explain why impossible cases are impossible.
z-m-16-02.material: At one bus stop, the bus on route 가 leaves every 12 minutes and the bus on route 나 leaves every 18 minutes. Today at 9 a.m. sharp the two buses left together, and after that each route keeps its interval exactly and keeps leaving. Harin said, "After 12×18=216 minutes, multiplying the two intervals, that is, at 12:36 p.m., they will leave together again for the first time!"
z-m-16-02.thinking.0: Telling apart 'in common' and 'first' in someone else's answer
z-m-16-02.thinking.1: Making several cases that satisfy the conditions
z-m-16-02.thinking.2: Explaining why something is not possible
z-m-16-02.prereq.0: The meaning of multiples, and writing the multiples of a number in order
z-m-16-02.prereq.1: Calculating with times in hours and minutes (changing minutes into a time of day)
z-m-16-02.s.s1.prompt: You looked at what Harin said. Choose the most suitable evaluation.
z-m-16-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write the times (in minutes) at which route 가 leaves, like 12, 24, ..., and write route 나 separately.
z-m-16-02.s.s1.o.a: After 12+18=30 minutes, the sum of the two intervals, is when they next leave together for the first time
z-m-16-02.s.s1.r.a: Check whether route 가 leaves after 30 minutes. Route 가 leaves at 12-minute intervals.
z-m-16-02.s.s1.o.b: They leave together for the first time after 18 minutes, the longer interval
z-m-16-02.s.s1.r.b: Route 나 leaves after 18 minutes. Check whether route 가 leaves at 18 minutes.
z-m-16-02.s.s1.o.c: After 216 minutes is right. The time found by multiplying the two intervals is when they leave together for the first time.
z-m-16-02.s.s1.r.c: It is true that both routes leave at the multiplied number. But did you check that there is no earlier time when they leave together?
z-m-16-02.s.s1.r.d: You told apart 'a time when both routes leave' from 'the first time both routes leave.'
z-m-16-02.s.s1.explain: The multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36, ... and the multiples of 18 are 18, 36, 54, ..., so they leave together for the first time after 36 minutes (at 9:36). 216 minutes is 6 times 36, so they leave together then too, but it is not the 'first' time.
z-m-16-02.s.s2.prompt: Here is a plan for new routes. The two routes leave together at 9 a.m., and the next time they leave together for the first time is to be 9:36 (36 minutes later). Decide route 가's interval a minutes and route 나's interval b minutes. a and b are natural numbers from 2 to 36, and a must be smaller than b. Find 3 different (a, b).
z-m-16-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one pair such as a=6, b=9, write the times each route leaves, and find the first time they coincide.
z-m-16-02.s.s2.hint.1: Compare what you should change if the first coinciding time is earlier than 36 minutes and what you should change if it is later than 36 minutes.
z-m-16-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be natural numbers from 2 to 36 with a<b.
z-m-16-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The first time they leave together is exactly 36 minutes later.
z-m-16-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The first time they leave together is not 36 minutes later. Write the multiples of the two intervals in order and check.
z-m-16-02.s.s2.explain: For example, for (4, 9), the multiples of 4 (4, 8, ..., 36) and the multiples of 9 (9, 18, 27, 36) first meet at 36. (12, 18) is the original situation. Pairs that meet at a time earlier than 36 ((6, 9) meets at 18 minutes) or pairs that fall short of 36 ((5, 7) meets at 35 minutes) do not fit the conditions.
z-m-16-02.s.s3.prompt: If route 나's interval is 8 minutes, can you make them leave together for the first time at 9:36 however you set route 가's interval? Write your judgment and reason.
z-m-16-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write the times route 나 (8-minute interval) leaves, like 8, 16, ....
z-m-16-02.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether 36 is among those times.
z-m-16-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is your reason explained by route 나 (8-minute interval) alone, or is it a story about trying several route 가 intervals?
z-m-16-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say whether route 나 leaves at 36 minutes?
z-m-16-02.s.s3.model.0: It is impossible. Route 나 leaves at 0, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40 minutes, so it does not leave at 36 minutes. This is because 36 is not a multiple of 8.
z-m-16-02.s.s3.model.1: It can't be done. 36÷8 is 4.5, so it does not divide evenly. If route 나 does not leave at 36 minutes, no matter what you do with route 가, they cannot leave together at 36 minutes.
z-m-16-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: Another method that explains it with division

z-m-16-03.title: Finding ranges of consecutive integers whose sum is 10
z-m-16-03.goal: Use the property that opposite numbers add up to 0 in sums of consecutive integers mixing positive and negative numbers, to find several ranges that fit the conditions and explain why.
z-m-16-03.material: Let 'S(s, e)' be the value found by adding all the integers one by one from the integer s to e (s is an integer not greater than e). For example, if s=−2 and e=3, it is (−2)+(−1)+0+1+2+3=3. 0 is also an integer, and s and e are also added.
z-m-16-03.thinking.0: Discovering a structure that shortens the calculation
z-m-16-03.thinking.1: Finding several solutions that satisfy the constraints
z-m-16-03.thinking.2: Explaining in words the method you discovered
z-m-16-03.prereq.1: The sum of two numbers with the same absolute value and opposite signs
z-m-16-03.s.s1.prompt: What is S(−3, 5), that is, the value of adding all the integers from −3 to 5? Choose while thinking about whether there is a way to find it without adding one by one.
z-m-16-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write all the numbers from −3 to 5 and connect with lines the numbers that have the same absolute value.
z-m-16-03.s.s1.hint.1: Add together only the numbers that are not connected.
z-m-16-03.s.s1.r.a: Can you explain how you used the numbers that pair up? If you solved it that way, you saw the structure well.
z-m-16-03.s.s1.r.b: This is the value of adding only the two end numbers, −3 and 5. You must add the middle numbers too.
z-m-16-03.s.s1.r.c: This is the value of adding only the positive numbers 1 to 5. The negative numbers and 0 are added too.
z-m-16-03.s.s1.r.d: From −3 to 3 they cancel each other out, but 4 and 5 are left over.
z-m-16-03.s.s1.explain: −3 and 3, −2 and 2, −1 and 1 add up to 0, and adding 0 changes nothing. Adding the leftover 4 and 5 gives 9.
z-m-16-03.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different (s, e), with s and e integers from −20 to 20 (s not greater than e), such that S(s, e) is exactly 10.
z-m-16-03.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a starting number and increase the ending number by 1 at a time, writing the sums in order.
z-m-16-03.s.s2.hint.1: See which numbers cancel each other out if you start including negative numbers.
z-m-16-03.s.s2.ok.c1: s and e are integers from −20 to 20, and s is not greater than e.
z-m-16-03.s.s2.fail.c1: s and e are integers from −20 to 20, and s cannot be greater than e.
z-m-16-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum from s to e is 10.
z-m-16-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The value of adding everything from s to e is not 10. Also check how many numbers you are adding.
z-m-16-03.s.s2.explain: In this range, the ranges whose sum is 10 are these four: (1, 4), (0, 4), (10, 10), (−9, 10). (−9, 10) is the case where −9 to 9 cancel each other out and only 10 is left.
z-m-16-03.s.s3.prompt: Explain why S(−9, 10)=10 without adding all 20 numbers.
z-m-16-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write all the numbers from −9 to 10 and pair up the ones with the same absolute value.
z-m-16-03.s.s3.hint.1: Look for any number that could not be paired.
z-m-16-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write specifically which numbers pair with which?
z-m-16-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write which number is left without a partner and why it is left?
z-m-16-03.s.s3.model.0: Numbers with the same absolute value and opposite signs, like −9 and 9, −8 and 8, add up to 0. Adding 0 changes nothing, and only 10, which has no partner, is left, so the sum is 10.
z-m-16-03.s.s3.model.1: The negative numbers −9 to −1 pair up one by one with the positive numbers 1 to 9 and all add up to 0. What is left is 0 and 10, so the sum is 10.
z-m-16-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: It wrote specifically the range that was paired up.

z-m-16-04.title: Choosing the coefficient so the solution is a natural number
z-m-16-04.topic: Solutions of linear equations and coefficients
z-m-16-04.goal: Test how the solution changes when the coefficient of an equation changes, design several coefficients that give a natural-number solution, and explain why other cases do not work.
z-m-16-04.material: There is the equation ax+6=2x+12 (a times x plus 6 equals 2x plus 12). a is an integer, and the solution x changes with a. We want to find a for which the solution is a 'natural number' (1, 2, 3, ...).
z-m-16-04.thinking.0: Observing how the solution changes when the coefficient changes
z-m-16-04.thinking.1: Making several designs that satisfy the conditions
z-m-16-04.thinking.2: Telling apart the case with no solution from the case where the solution is not a natural number
z-m-16-04.prereq.0: Solving linear equations (moving terms, dividing both sides by the same number)
z-m-16-04.prereq.1: The meaning of natural numbers, integers, and divisors
z-m-16-04.s.s1.prompt: When a=2, what is the solution of the equation 2x+6=2x+12?
z-m-16-04.s.s1.hint.0: Subtract the same term from both sides and simplify.
z-m-16-04.s.s1.hint.1: Look at whether the simplified equation is true or false regardless of x.
z-m-16-04.s.s1.r.a: If you put x=0 into both sides, you get 6=12. Check whether it holds.
z-m-16-04.s.s1.r.b: Put 6 in for x and calculate both sides. Are the two values equal?
z-m-16-04.s.s1.r.c: You found that there is no x at all that makes both sides equal. Tell how this result comes out.
z-m-16-04.s.s1.r.d: If you remove 2x from both sides, 6 and 12 are left. Are the two values equal?
z-m-16-04.s.s1.explain: If you subtract 2x from both sides, you get 6=12, which is false regardless of x. So no x can be a solution.
z-m-16-04.s.s2.prompt: When a and x are both integers and x is a natural number, find 3 pairs (a, x) with different a for which ax+6=2x+12 holds. (a is from −20 to 20)
z-m-16-04.s.s2.hint.0: Put small integers in for a one at a time, solve the equation, and check whether the solution is a natural number.
z-m-16-04.s.s2.hint.1: Organize in a table for which a the solution is negative and for which a it is a fraction.
z-m-16-04.s.s2.ok.c1: a is an integer from −20 to 20.
z-m-16-04.s.s2.fail.c1: a must be an integer from −20 to 20.
z-m-16-04.s.s2.fail.c2: x is not a natural number (1, 2, 3, ...).
z-m-16-04.s.s2.fail.c3: When you put x and a into the equation, the two sides are not equal. Calculate and check.
z-m-16-04.s.s2.explain: When a is 3, 4, 5, 8, x is 6, 3, 2, 1. If a=0, x=−3 (not a natural number), and if a=6, x=1.5 (not an integer), so they do not work.
z-m-16-04.s.s3.hint.0: In ax+6=2x+12, gather the terms containing x on one side.
z-m-16-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say what relation a−2 must have with 6 for the solution to be a natural number?
z-m-16-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does your judgment for a=1000 connect to your reason for a=7?
z-m-16-04.s.s3.model.0: (a−2)x=6, so x=6÷(a−2). If a=7, it is 6÷5, which is not a natural number. It is a natural number only when a−2 is a divisor of 6, and if a=1000, a−2=998, so it does not work.
z-m-16-04.s.s3.model.1: (a−2) times x must be 6. There is no natural number that gives 6 when multiplied by 5, so a=7 does not work. If a=1000, a−2 is 998, and multiplying it by any natural number makes it greater than 6, so it does not work.
z-m-16-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: Another method that explains it with multiplication

z-m-16-05.title: Discounts and coupons: does the value change with the order you use them?
z-m-16-05.topic: Comparing two methods with an expression with a letter
z-m-16-05.goal: Calculate and compare the values of two methods at several prices, use the letter x to express the difference and check that there is a constant difference regardless of price, and examine the range in which that expression holds.
z-m-16-05.material: You want to buy an item with list price x원 at an online shop. At first, we look at the case where x is an integer that is 2000 or more. There are two discounts: '20% off' (the price becomes 0.8 times) and a '1000원 coupon' (subtract 1000원 from the price). You use each discount once, but you can choose the order. Method A is to take the 20% off first and then use the 1000원 coupon on that price, and method B is to use the 1000원 coupon first and then take the 20% off that price.
z-m-16-05.thinking.0: Guessing a rule from examples and adjusting how sure you are
z-m-16-05.thinking.1: Comparing two methods with an expression with a letter
z-m-16-05.thinking.2: Examining the condition (range) under which an expression holds
z-m-16-05.prereq.0: Expressing a percent discount as 0.8 times
z-m-16-05.prereq.1: Simple calculation with expressions containing the letter x (collecting like terms)
z-m-16-05.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what is closest to what you think now.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.hint.0: At each stage, tell apart the 'list prices you have already checked' from the 'list prices you have not checked yet.'
z-m-16-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare which parts are the same and which are different in the calculations that gave the values of the two methods.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: For an item with a list price of 10000원, will the same method also be cheaper? What is closest to what you think now?
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.after: The result at one list price cannot settle other prices. Both the expectation that the same side will be cheaper and the doubt that it could flip are thoughts worth testing.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A will be cheaper. Even if the list price changes, the same side seems likely to be cheaper.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You expected that a result seen at one price will carry over to other prices. You can check by changing the list price and calculating.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: If the list price changes, B could become cheaper
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You left open the point that one example can flip a judgment. You can find out by trying a different list price.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The values of the two methods are the same whatever the list price is
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: At 2000원 they were already different, 600원 and 800원. How can you check this example against this idea?
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: If we don't know the list price, we can't tell which is cheaper
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: If you pick one list price and calculate, you get a clue. Use the result for 2000원.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.info: When the list price is 10000원, A is 10000×0.8=8000 and 8000−1000=7000원. B is 10000−1000=9000 and 9000×0.8=7200원. As with 2000원, A is 200원 cheaper than B.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: How do you interpret this result?
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.after: That the difference is the same in the two examples is a clue that there may be a rule. It might be chance, so it is good to generalize with the letter x and check.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Coming out the same twice is chance, and at other list prices the difference will change
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: There is no ground to call it chance from just two cases either. If you check at other list prices, you can find out whether it is chance.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: At list prices of both 2000원 and 10000원, A is 200원 cheaper. I want to check whether it is the same at other list prices
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You took the same difference in the two examples as a clue, and said you would test with other list prices.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The difference of 200원 is the same as 20% of the 1000원 coupon, so it seems to be a value related to the order of using the coupon
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You guessed where the number 200 came from. You can check with an expression whether this guess is right.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The result that A is cheaper came out twice, so we don't need to check more
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You have only checked twice. You still don't know about other list prices (for example 4000원 or 100000원).
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.info: Let's write it with a letter. A's value is 0.8x−1000. B's value is (x−1000)×0.8, which simplifies to 0.8x−800.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: When the list price is x원, how much is the difference of B's value minus A's value?
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.after: (0.8x−800)−(0.8x−1000)=200. The terms containing x disappear, so whatever the list price is (in the range where the expressions hold), A is 200원 cheaper.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Both expressions contain 0.8x. Check what happens to 0.8x when you subtract.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It changes with the list price x
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Subtract the expressions yourself. Check whether any term containing x remains.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You found the difference by seeing that the parts containing x disappear in the two expressions.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is the value of A subtracted from B. Check whether the sign matches which one is more expensive.
z-m-16-05.s.s1.reflect: How did your thinking change when you had the result for one list price, the results for two, and then the expression with a letter? Even if you first chose 'a' or 'b,' what became more certain at the end?
z-m-16-05.s.s2.prompt: Suppose the coupon is 1500원 instead of 1000원 and the discount stays 20%. When the list price is 4000원, how much is the difference of B's value minus A's value?
z-m-16-05.s.s2.hint.0: Calculate A's value and B's value separately.
z-m-16-05.s.s2.hint.1: Compare how the coupon amount of 1500원 goes into A's expression and into B's expression.
z-m-16-05.s.s2.r.a: You calculated A and B separately and found the difference, or you worked out how the coupon amount shows up in the difference. What if you replaced the coupon amount with c원?
z-m-16-05.s.s2.r.b: You carried over the difference for the 1000원 coupon as it is. Calculate directly whether the difference changes when the coupon amount changes.
z-m-16-05.s.s2.r.c: It looks like you fitted a value without finding out how the difference arises. Calculate A and B separately.
z-m-16-05.s.s2.r.d: You used the coupon amount as the difference as it is. Is the difference that arises from the different order of using the coupon equal to the coupon amount?
z-m-16-05.s.s2.explain: A is 4000×0.8−1500=1700원, and B is (4000−1500)×0.8=2000원. The difference is 300원, which is 20% of the coupon amount 1500원. If the coupon is c원, the difference is 0.2×c원.
z-m-16-05.s.s3.prompt: For an item with a list price of 1100원, can we still say 'A is 200원 cheaper than B'? (Assume a price cannot go below 0원, and a coupon can only be used up to the amount of the price remaining.) Calculate the values of the two methods when the list price is 1100원, and write your judgment and reason.
z-m-16-05.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate A's value and B's value when the list price is 1100원.
z-m-16-05.s.s3.hint.1: Look at what happens if you subtract the 1000원 coupon from A's intermediate value.
z-m-16-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Do the values of A and B you calculated fit the assumption of the problem (not going below 0원)?
z-m-16-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state the range, 'up to when the 200원 rule is right'?
z-m-16-05.s.s3.model.0: No. At 1100원, A is 1100×0.8=880원, but the coupon is 1000원, so only 880원 of it can be used, and the price becomes 0원, while B is (1100−1000)×0.8=80원. The difference is 80원, not 200원.
z-m-16-05.s.s3.model.1: It doesn't hold. The 200원 difference is right only when the whole 1000원 coupon can be used. If the list price is lower than 1250원, part of the coupon is left over in A and the price cannot go below 0원, so the difference becomes smaller.

z-m-16-06.title: A 3×3 block on a calendar: what numbers can the sum be?
z-m-16-06.topic: A rule written with a letter and the range of possible values
z-m-16-06.goal: Guess how the sum of a 3×3 block on a calendar relates to the middle date and find the reason, then consider both the conditions on the numbers and the conditions of the calendar layout to sort out which sums are possible and which are impossible.
z-m-16-06.material:
On a calendar, you will pick a 3×3 block (3 squares across, 3 squares down) in which every square has a date, and add all 9 dates. You cannot pick a block that has even one blank square or whose squares wrap onto a different row.
This month's calendar (the 1st is a Thursday and the month has 31 days) is as follows. Each row is in the order Sun, Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat.
First row: (4 blank squares) 1, 2, 3
Second row: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10
Third row: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17
Fourth row: 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24
Fifth row: 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31 (no blank squares)
z-m-16-06.thinking.0: Examining the reason before generalizing a rule from one example
z-m-16-06.thinking.1: Considering conditions on numbers and conditions on layout together
z-m-16-06.thinking.2: Sorting out impossible values together with reasons
z-m-16-06.prereq.0: Expressing a rule with an expression using a letter
z-m-16-06.prereq.1: Reading the days of the week and the arrangement of dates on a calendar
z-m-16-06.s.s1.prompt: The sum of the block whose middle date is 15 (7, 8, 9 / 14, 15, 16 / 21, 22, 23) is 135. Among the ways to find the sum of the block whose middle date is 20 (12, 13, 14 / 19, 20, 21 / 26, 27, 28), choose the one that can explain the reason using only facts already known.
z-m-16-06.s.s1.hint.0: Pair up the dates of the two blocks by the same position and write how much each changed.
z-m-16-06.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the amount changed is the same for all 9 squares.
z-m-16-06.s.s1.o.a: All 9 squares became 5 larger, so use 135+5×9=180
z-m-16-06.s.s1.r.a: You compared the same positions of the two blocks and used the fact that every one became 5 larger. This is a method that can explain the reason.
z-m-16-06.s.s1.r.b: The dates of the block with 20 in the middle are all greater than the dates of the block with 15 in the middle. Could the sums be the same?
z-m-16-06.s.s1.o.c: The sum was 15×9, so it is 9 times the middle date; use 20×9=180
z-m-16-06.s.s1.r.c: The answer is the same, but you used a rule seen once at 15 without a reason. You need to check that it also holds for other middle dates.
z-m-16-06.s.s1.r.d: All 9 squares became 5 larger. If you add 5 only once, how many squares would have grown?
z-m-16-06.s.s1.explain: The 9 dates of the block with 20 in the middle are each 5 larger than the dates of the block with 15 in the middle (7→12, 8→13, ..., 23→28). So the sum is 135+5×9=180. It is also the same as 20×9=180, 9 times the middle date.
z-m-16-06.s.s1.acc.0: The result 180 is right. However, it used a rule seen once at 15 (9 times the middle date) without a reason, so a further step of checking whether it holds for other middle dates or finding the reason is needed.
z-m-16-06.s.s2.prompt: Enter the middle date c of a 3×3 block on the calendar above in which every square has a date, and the sum s of its 9 squares. Find 3 different c such that the sum s is from 150 to 200.
z-m-16-06.s.s2.hint.0: First mark which dates on the calendar can be the middle of a 3×3 block.
z-m-16-06.s.s2.hint.1: For each of those middle dates, find the sum of the 9 squares and pick the ones that fall between 150 and 200.
z-m-16-06.s.s2.fail.c1: c and s must be integers.
z-m-16-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The 3×3 block with that date in the middle is within the calendar.
z-m-16-06.s.s2.fail.c2: If you make that date the middle, there are blank squares or squares that wrap onto another row. Look again at the shape of the calendar.
z-m-16-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The sum of the 9 dates is right.
z-m-16-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum of the 9 dates is not right. Add again.
z-m-16-06.s.s2.fail.c4: The sum is not from 150 to 200.
z-m-16-06.s.s2.explain: If the middle date is 19, 20, 21, 22, the sums are 171, 180, 189, 198. 17 is a Saturday, so its right-hand square wraps onto the next row, 16 has a sum of 144, which is less than 150, and 23 has a sum of 207, which is greater than 200.
z-m-16-06.s.s3.prompt: On this calendar, could there be a 3×3 block with sum 99 and a 3×3 block with sum 100? Judge each and write the reasons.
z-m-16-06.s.s3.hint.0: Recall how the sum related to the middle date and apply it to 99 and to 100 separately.
z-m-16-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you tell apart that the reasons for 100 and 99 are of different kinds (a property of numbers / the calendar layout)?
z-m-16-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you avoid concluding 'there is one' just from the fact that 99 is a multiple of 9?
z-m-16-06.s.s3.model.0: There is none for 100. The sum is 9 times the middle date, so it must be a multiple of 9, but 100 is not a multiple of 9. 99 is a multiple of 9, but the middle would have to be 11, and 11 is in the Sunday column, so there is no square to its left in the same row and a 3×3 block cannot be made. So there is none for either.
z-m-16-06.s.s3.model.1: Both are impossible. The sum is 9 times the middle date, so for 99 the middle would be 11, and 100 is not divisible by 9. 11 is at the edge of the calendar (Sunday), so a 3×3 block can't be made.
z-m-16-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: It briefly wrote both reasons, multiples and layout.

z-m-16-07.title: A round trip with different speeds going and coming back: what is the average speed?
z-m-16-07.topic: Speed, time, distance, and expressions with letters
z-m-16-07.goal: Examine with examples and an expression with a letter whether the result is fixed even when the distance is not given, and understand which quantity you divide by when finding an average.
z-m-16-07.material: Jiho walks from home to the library at 4km per hour (4km in 1 hour) and walks back along the same road at 6km per hour. She does not rest on either part, and her speed is constant. The 'round-trip average speed' is defined as (total distance of the round trip)÷(total time the round trip took). The distance between home and the library is not given.
z-m-16-07.thinking.0: Judging what information is needed in a problem that seems to lack information
z-m-16-07.thinking.1: Generalizing from examples to an expression with a letter
z-m-16-07.thinking.2: Finding an error in a solution through a contradiction in the result
z-m-16-07.prereq.0: Understanding the relation distance = speed × time
z-m-16-07.prereq.1: Addition of fractions (finding a common denominator)
z-m-16-07.prereq.2: Setting up an expression containing the letter d
z-m-16-07.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what is closest to what you think now.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.hint.0: Pick a distance and calculate the time taken going and the time taken coming back.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.hint.1: Change the distance, calculate once more, and compare the results.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.0.info: We don't know the distance yet. She walks at 4km per hour going and 6km per hour coming back.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think now about the round-trip average speed?
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.0.after: We don't know the distance yet, so it is too early to give an exact value. Both the guess that it is between 4 and 6 and the thought that the distance seems to be needed can be tested.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It will be 5km per hour, exactly in the middle of 4 and 6
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Is there a reason you see it as exactly in the middle? That means you took the time walking at 4km/h and the time walking at 6km/h to be the same.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It seems to be a value between 4 and 6, but we need to find out more to get the exact value
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: The intuition that it lies between the speeds of the two parts is reasonable. You also thought about what is needed to get the exact value.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We don't know the distance, so it seems we can't find the average speed either
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: It is natural that the distance seems needed. If you assume a distance and calculate, you can check whether it is really needed.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It will be faster than 6km per hour
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: It is the value of the whole round trip divided by the time taken. Think about whether it could be faster than the fastest speed.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.1.info: Let's assume the distance is 12km. Going takes 12÷4=3 hours and coming back takes 12÷6=2 hours. So she went a round trip of 24km in 5 hours.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: What is the round-trip average speed, in km per hour, then?
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.1.after: 24÷5=4.8. The average speed is not the average of the two speeds but the total distance divided by the total time.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: 5 is exactly in the middle of 4 and 6. Divide it yourself to see how many km per hour it is if she went 24km in 5 hours.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Look at how you got that value. Calculate 24÷5.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Calculate 24÷5 again. Check whether it matches this value.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You divided the total round-trip distance by the total time. You did not simply average the speeds of the parts.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.2.info: If the distance is 24km, going takes 24÷4=6 hours and coming back takes 24÷6=4 hours, so it takes 10 hours, and the round trip is 48km. The average speed is 48÷10=4.8, which is 4.8km per hour.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: Let's go back to the beginning. When you don't know the distance, what would you say about the round-trip average speed?
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.2.after: It was 4.8km/h both times, so it is likely to be the same regardless of distance. Before checking by calling the distance the letter d, it is too early to say it is the same for every distance.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It can be found only if we know the distance
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: It was 4.8 for both 12km and 24km. How can you explain that the result was the same even though the distance was different?
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It was 4.8 in both cases, so it seems to be 4.8 regardless of distance
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You took the same value coming out in two examples as a clue. You need to check with a letter whether it holds for every distance.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The longer the distance, the greater the average speed
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The average speed was the same for 12km and for 24km. It did not get greater.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.2.o.d: I have only looked at two cases, so I want to call the distance d km and check whether it is the same for every distance
z-m-16-07.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is the attitude of checking with a letter before generalizing from two examples.
z-m-16-07.s.s1.reflect: How did your thinking change at the first guess, when you assumed the distance was 12km, and when you assumed 24km? It was a 'problem where you don't know the distance,' but was the distance really needed?
z-m-16-07.s.s2.prompt: This is Jiho's solution, calculated by calling the distance d km. Choose one line that cannot be trusted. (You may choose a line with a wrong calculation, or a line where a wrong conclusion is written because of it.)
z-m-16-07.s.s2.hint.0: Compare the result of this solution with the result calculated earlier with 12km.
z-m-16-07.s.s2.hint.1: Check line by line whether each line follows from the line just before it, recalculating each line.
z-m-16-07.s.s2.line.0: Let the distance from home to the library be d km.
z-m-16-07.s.s2.line.1: The time going is d÷4=d/4 (hours), and the time coming back is d÷6=d/6 (hours).
z-m-16-07.s.s2.line.2: The total time for the round trip is d/4+d/6=2d/10=d/5 (hours).
z-m-16-07.s.s2.line.3: The round-trip distance is 2d km, so the average speed is 2d÷(d/5)=10 (km/h).
z-m-16-07.s.s2.line.4: Therefore, whatever the distance, the average speed is 10km per hour.
z-m-16-07.s.s2.explain: The mistake is in line 3. d/4+d/6 should be made to have the same denominator: 3d/12+2d/12=5d/12 (hours). You must not add the numerators together and the denominators together. Then the average speed is 2d÷(5d/12)=24/5=4.8 (km/h), and d cancels out, so it is the same regardless of distance. The 10km/h in lines 4 and 5 is a result that carries over the error in line 3, and it differs from the 4.8 found earlier, so you can doubt it. The direction 'it does not depend on the distance' is right.
z-m-16-07.s.s3.prompt: Write why the round-trip average speed is 4.8, less than 5, rather than 5, exactly in the middle of 4 and 6, paying attention to the time going and the time coming back.
z-m-16-07.s.s3.hint.0: Compare the time taken going and the time taken coming back.
z-m-16-07.s.s3.hint.1: Check at which speed she walks for longer, and think about which side the average gets closer to.
z-m-16-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you connect the fact that 'the time is longer' with the conclusion that 'the average is close to the slower one'?
z-m-16-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: If you gave a concrete example like 12km, did you write values like 3 hours going and 2 hours coming back correctly?
z-m-16-07.s.s3.model.0: Going, when she walks slowly, takes longer. Of the total time, more is spent walking at 4km per hour, so the average is 4.8, leaning toward 4 rather than 5.
z-m-16-07.s.s3.model.1: When the distance is 12km, going takes 3 hours and coming back takes 2 hours. The time walking at 4km per hour is longer, so that speed affects the average more, and it becomes less than 5.
z-m-16-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: It explained with a concrete example.

z-m-16-08.title: Can we call this correspondence a function?
z-m-16-08.topic: The meaning of a function (a correspondence that is decided one by one)
z-m-16-08.goal: Decide whether something is a function by whether exactly one value of y is decided for each value of x, show with a counterexample a correspondence that is not a function, and explain why different values of x may have the same y.
z-m-16-08.material: A rule that pairs a value of y with each value you choose for x is called a 'correspondence.' In a correspondence, when exactly one value of y is decided for each value of x, y is called a function of x. (If, once the value of x is chosen, two or more values of y come out, it is not a function.)
z-m-16-08.thinking.0: Checking the conditions of a definition one by one
z-m-16-08.thinking.1: Making a counterexample to show something is not a function
z-m-16-08.thinking.2: Telling apart what is allowed from what is not allowed
z-m-16-08.prereq.0: The meaning of natural numbers, divisors, multiples, and remainders
z-m-16-08.prereq.1: The meaning of a correspondence as 'a rule that pairs values of y with values of x'
z-m-16-08.s.s1.prompt: When x is a natural number, choose all the correspondences below in which y is a function of x.
z-m-16-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put in a few small natural numbers for x and write in a table how many y come out.
z-m-16-08.s.s1.hint.1: Look for whether there is even one x for which two or more y come out.
z-m-16-08.s.s1.o.a: Let y be a divisor of x
z-m-16-08.s.s1.r.a: When x=6, y is several values: 1, 2, 3, 6. Count how many y correspond to one x.
z-m-16-08.s.s1.o.b: Let y be the remainder when x is divided by 6
z-m-16-08.s.s1.r.b: Once x is chosen, the remainder is decided as one value. If you chose this after checking that, you applied the definition well.
z-m-16-08.s.s1.o.c: Let y be a natural number smaller than x
z-m-16-08.s.s1.r.c: When x=4, y is several values: 1, 2, 3.
z-m-16-08.s.s1.o.d: Let y be the number that is 1 more than 2 times x
z-m-16-08.s.s1.r.d: Once x is chosen, y is decided as the single value 2x+1.
z-m-16-08.s.s1.o.e: Let y be a multiple of x
z-m-16-08.s.s1.r.e: When x=3, y is several values: 3, 6, 9, ....
z-m-16-08.s.s1.explain: For b and d, y is decided as one value once x is chosen. For a, c, e, several y come out for one x, as with x=6, 4, 3, so they are not functions.
z-m-16-08.s.s2.prompt: For age x years and height y cm, it is said that 'the correspondence that picks one student and pairs that student's height y with that student's age x' is not a function. Make 2 different examples showing the reason. Enter the (age, height) of two students of the same age. (Age is an integer from 8 to 19 and height is an integer from 120 to 200, and the first student's height y1 must be less than the second student's height y2.)
z-m-16-08.s.s2.hint.0: First think of two students of the same age, and set their heights to be different.
z-m-16-08.s.s2.hint.1: Check that both conditions, the same age and different heights, are kept.
z-m-16-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Age must be an integer from 8 to 19 and height an integer from 120 to 200.
z-m-16-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The two students have the same age.
z-m-16-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The two students must have the same age.
z-m-16-08.s.s2.ok.c3: The two students have different heights.
z-m-16-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The first student's height must be less than the second student's height (they must be different).
z-m-16-08.s.s2.explain: If there are several 13-year-old students with heights 155cm and 162cm, then y is not decided as one value for x=13. So this correspondence is not a function. Students of different ages cannot be a counterexample.
z-m-16-08.s.s3.prompt: When x is a natural number, if 'y is the remainder when x is divided by 6,' then y=1 when x=7 and y=1 when x=13 too. Does different values of x having the same y go against the condition of a function? Write your judgment and reason.
z-m-16-08.s.s3.hint.0: Count how many y there are when x=7 and how many y there are when x=13.
z-m-16-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say whether there is only one y when x=7, and whether there is only one y when x=13?
z-m-16-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart 'the same y appears twice' from 'two y for one x'?
z-m-16-08.s.s3.model.0: It does not go against it. A function only needs exactly one y decided for each x. When x=7, y is only 1, and when x=13, it is also only 1, so it is fine.
z-m-16-08.s.s3.model.1: No problem. The rule only checks whether exactly one y comes out once x is chosen, so different x may use the same y. On the other hand, if two y come out for one x, it is not a function.
z-m-16-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: It also stated the opposite case.

z-m-16-09.title: Is the direct proportion graph with the larger a always above?
z-m-16-09.topic: Comparing values of the direct proportion y=ax
z-m-16-09.goal: Check with examples that the result of comparing the values of two direct proportions y=ax and y=bx changes with the sign of x, revise the claim by adding a condition, and make a counterexample yourself.
z-m-16-09.material: On one coordinate plane, you drew the graph of y=3x (3 times x) and the graph of y=2x. A friend said, "For the same x, the value of y=3x is always greater than the value of y=2x. So the graph of y=3x is always higher!" (There is no picture. A graph being 'above' means that for the same x, the value of y is greater. You can put numbers in for x and compare the two values of y.)
z-m-16-09.thinking.0: Testing a claim obtained from some examples
z-m-16-09.thinking.1: Finding the condition (sign of x) and revising the claim
z-m-16-09.thinking.2: Making a counterexample with a condition attached
z-m-16-09.prereq.0: Putting numbers in for x in the direct proportion y=ax to find y (including negative numbers)
z-m-16-09.prereq.1: Multiplication of negative numbers and comparing the sizes of numbers
z-m-16-09.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what is closest to what you think now.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.hint.0: At each stage, tell apart the kinds of x you have checked (positive, 0, negative).
z-m-16-09.s.s1.hint.1: For the same x, write the values of the two expressions side by side and compare which is greater.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.0.info: When x=1, y=3x is 3 and y=2x is 2. When x=2, they are 6 and 4, and when x=5, they are 15 and 10.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think now about your friend's claim, 'For the same x, the value of y=3x is always greater'?
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.0.after: The x you checked are all positive. To say 'always,' you need to check x that are not positive too.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It was right in all three cases, so it is right for all x
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The x you checked are only 1, 2, and 5. Did you check x that are 0, negative, or decimals too?
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We should test x that are 0 or negative too
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You noticed that all the x checked are positive and said you would test other kinds of x.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.0.o.c: 3 is greater than 2, so it is always right without needing to check
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: It is true that the coefficient is greater, but whether the result of multiplying by x is also always greater depends on the value of x.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It is only so when x is large, and when x is small it must be wrong
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: There is not yet any evidence that it is wrong for small x. You can find out by calculating directly.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.1.info: When x=0, the two values are 0 and 0, the same. When x=−1, y=3x is −3 and y=2x is −2. When x=−4, they are −12 and −8.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: What do you think now about your friend's claim?
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.1.after: When x is positive, 3x is greater than 2x; at x=0 they are equal; and when x is negative, 3x is less than 2x. 'Always' is false, and you must attach the condition 'when x is positive.'
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Negative numbers are a special case, so the claim is right as it is
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: A negative x is also a value of x. The words 'for the same x, always' include negative x.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The two values are equal at x=0, so the claim is wrong and there is nothing more to fix
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It is right that they are equal at x=0. But you can also work out in which range the claim holds.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Only when x is positive is 3x greater, so the claim should be revised to 'when x is positive'
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You separated the range where the claim holds from the range where it does not.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.1.o.d: For negative x, 3x is smaller, so now we should say y=3x is always smaller
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.1.r.d: When x=1, 3x was 3 and 2x was 2, so 3x was greater. This opposite claim does not hold either.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.2.info: Let's compare two other relations, y=−x and y=−2x. When x=3, they are −3 and −6, and when x=−3, they are 3 and 6. Here −1 is a number greater than −2.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: When a is a number greater than b, what is the most suitable explanation of which of y=ax and y=bx has the greater value?
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.2.after: When a>b, if x>0 then ax>bx, if x<0 then ax<bx, and if x=0 they are equal. This is because multiplying by a negative number reverses the direction of the inequality sign.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.2.o.a: If a is greater than b, the value of y=ax is greater regardless of the sign of x
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.2.r.a: When x=−3, y=−x is 3 and y=−2x is 6. Compare these values.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Only when a and b are negative does the result change with the sign of x
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Even when they are positive, like a=3, b=2, the result changed at x=−1.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.2.o.c: If x is positive, y=bx is greater
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.2.r.c: When x=3, −x is −3 and −2x is −6. Which is greater?
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.2.o.d: If x is positive, y=ax is greater, and if x is negative, y=bx is greater
z-m-16-09.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This agrees with comparing the two values at x=3 and x=−3.
z-m-16-09.s.s1.reflect: How did your thinking change as the results for x=1, 2, 5, the results for 0 and negative numbers, and the results for y=−x and y=−2x came out? How far do you need to check when you use the word 'always'?
z-m-16-09.s.s2.prompt: Make an example where the statement 'If a is greater than b, the value of y=ax is always greater than the value of y=bx' is wrong. Enter (a, b, x) with a, b, x integers from −9 to −1, a>b, the value of y=ax less than the value of y=bx, and both values greater than 0, for 3 different (a, b).
z-m-16-09.s.s2.hint.0: First choose pairs with a>b by putting integers from −9 to −1 in for a and b.
z-m-16-09.s.s2.hint.1: Put several x into the pair you chose, calculate ax and bx, and find an x that fits the conditions.
z-m-16-09.s.s2.ok.c1: a, b, and x are integers from −9 to −1.
z-m-16-09.s.s2.fail.c1: a, b, and x must be integers from −9 to −1.
z-m-16-09.s.s2.fail.c2: a must be greater than b.
z-m-16-09.s.s2.ok.c3: The value of y=ax is less than the value of y=bx.
z-m-16-09.s.s2.fail.c3: When you put in x, the value of y=ax is not less than the value of y=bx.
z-m-16-09.s.s2.fail.c4: The two values are not both greater than 0.
z-m-16-09.s.s2.explain: If a and b are negative, a>b, and x is also negative, then ax and bx are both positive, but because we multiplied by a negative number and |a|<|b|, ax<bx. For example, with (−1, −2, −3), ax=3 and bx=6.
z-m-16-09.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite 'The graph of y=3x is always above the graph of y=2x' into a true statement. Write the revised sentence and, as its evidence, give at least one value of x in numbers.
z-m-16-09.s.s3.hint.0: Recall the results you checked above for x=−1, 0, 2.
z-m-16-09.s.s3.hint.1: Write in sentences the x for which the claim holds and the x for which it does not.
z-m-16-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it clear in your revised sentence for which x it holds?
z-m-16-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you actually compare the two values of y at the x you gave?
z-m-16-09.s.s3.model.0: It must be revised to say that only when x is positive is y=3x above y=2x. For example, if x=2 they are 6 and 4, but if x=−2 they are −6 and −4, so 3x is lower.
z-m-16-09.s.s3.model.1: You must attach the condition 'when x is greater than 0.' At x=0 both are 0 and equal, and at x=−1 they are −3 and −2, so the claim breaks.
z-m-16-09.s.s3.modelNote.1: It also checked the boundary value x=0.

z-m-16-10.title: Can we say the paper thickness measured with a ruler is directly proportional?
z-m-16-10.topic: Checking a direct proportion (measured values and error)
z-m-16-10.goal: Taking into account that measured values have error, judge 'can it be a direct proportion even if the ratios are not exactly the same?', sort out whether new data agrees with the model, and plan how to check further.
z-m-16-10.material:
You stacked x sheets of the same paper and, using a ruler with 1mm marks, read the nearest mark and recorded the thickness y mm. It is said that the value read differs from the real thickness by 0.5mm or less. Assume that all the paper is the same and does not get squashed when stacked.
Table (number of sheets x → thickness read y): 100 sheets → 10mm, 200 sheets → 21mm, 300 sheets → 31mm, 400 sheets → 41mm.
The values of y÷x are 0.1, 0.105, about 0.1033, and about 0.1025.
z-m-16-10.thinking.0: Judging while taking measurement error into account
z-m-16-10.thinking.1: Comparing whether new data agrees with the model
z-m-16-10.thinking.2: Deciding whether to change or keep a judgment and making a plan for further checks
z-m-16-10.prereq.0: The meaning of a=y÷x (the ratio) in the direct proportion y=ax
z-m-16-10.prereq.1: Multiplying decimals and rounding (reading the nearest mark)
z-m-16-10.s.s1.prompt: The values of y÷x differ slightly. Can we say the thickness is directly proportional to the number of sheets?
z-m-16-10.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate y÷x for all four columns and look at how much the values differ.
z-m-16-10.s.s1.r.a: If it were a direct proportion, y÷x would have to be exactly the same, but this y is a value read from the nearest mark. Think about how much a value read can differ from the real one.
z-m-16-10.s.s1.r.b: Is there evidence to think the other three values are all wrong? The values read can have an error of about 0.5mm.
z-m-16-10.s.s1.r.c: Growing together alone does not make it a direct proportion. You also need to check whether the ratio is constant.
z-m-16-10.s.s1.r.d: You judged taking the error into account. It becomes more certain if you check whether one ratio can really explain all four values.
z-m-16-10.s.s1.explain: A value read from the marks can differ from the real thickness by up to 0.5mm. If the ratio is 0.103, the thicknesses for 100, 200, 300, 400 sheets are 10.3, 20.6, 30.9, 41.2mm, and reading each at the nearest mark gives 10, 21, 31, 41mm. All four values in the table are explained, so there is a possibility that it is a direct proportion (it is not certain).
z-m-16-10.s.s2.prompt: Now let's believe that y=0.103x is right. The value read is said to differ from the real thickness by 0.5mm or less. Among the next newly measured values, choose all those that do not agree with this model and make you doubt the model.
z-m-16-10.s.s2.hint.0: First calculate the thickness the model gives for each number of sheets using y=0.103x.
z-m-16-10.s.s2.hint.1: Find how much the calculated thickness differs from the value read and compare it with 0.5mm.
z-m-16-10.s.s2.r.b: You found that the difference between the thickness the model gives and the value read is much greater than the reading error.
z-m-16-10.s.s2.r.c: The thickness the model gives is 5.15mm. Compare the difference from the value read with 0.5mm.
z-m-16-10.s.s2.r.d: The thickness the model gives is 61.8mm. Compare the difference from the value read with 0.5mm.
z-m-16-10.s.s2.r.e: You found that the difference between the thickness the model gives and the value read is much greater than the reading error.
z-m-16-10.s.s3.prompt: If you stacked 800 sheets and really read 90mm, what would you do about the judgment so far (that it may be a direct proportion)? Write your judgment, the reason, and one thing you would do to check.
z-m-16-10.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate the thickness the model gives for 800 sheets and compare it with the 90mm read.
z-m-16-10.s.s3.hint.1: After deciding whether the difference is explained by reading error, write what to do next to make the judgment more certain.
z-m-16-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is your judgment based on the difference between the 'value read' and the 'value the model gives'?
z-m-16-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Whether you change your judgment or keep it, is what you will check specific?
z-m-16-10.s.s3.model.0: If it were a direct proportion model, 800 sheets should be about 82mm, but 90 differs by nearly 8mm, so reading error cannot explain it. If you stack a lot, the stack might get squashed and change, so first I will measure 800 sheets again and also measure 600 and 700 sheets.
z-m-16-10.s.s3.model.1: I might have measured wrongly, so I will first measure again. If 90 still comes out, the difference from the model is too large, so I will conclude that although it was right up to 400 sheets, beyond that it is not a direct proportion, and I will measure more with different numbers of sheets.
z-m-16-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: It chose to hold off on judging and measure again first.

z-m-16-11.title: The time to drive 400km under a speed limit
z-m-16-11.topic: Inverse proportion formulas and properties of their graphs
z-m-16-11.goal: In a situation where speed and time taken are inversely proportional, compare the ratios of change, find several solutions that satisfy both conditions, and explain, using the product, why the time cannot be 0.
z-m-16-11.material: Assume the road distance from Seoul to Busan is 400km (it may differ from the real distance). If you drive without stopping at a constant speed of x km/h (x kilometers per hour), it takes y hours. The speed limit on this road is 100km/h, and you want to arrive within 5 hours.
z-m-16-11.thinking.0: Comparing ratios of change by changing the base
z-m-16-11.thinking.1: Finding values that satisfy several conditions at once
z-m-16-11.thinking.2: Explaining why a graph does not touch the axes
z-m-16-11.prereq.1: In the inverse proportion y=a/x, the product of x and y is constant
z-m-16-11.s.s1.prompt: If you raise the speed from 80km/h to 100km/h, the time taken drops from 5 hours to 4 hours. Which explanation correctly compares the changes in speed and time?
z-m-16-11.s.s1.hint.0: Write the speed and time at 80km/h and at 100km/h side by side and decide the base value for each.
z-m-16-11.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the amount changed with each one's own base value to find the ratio.
z-m-16-11.s.s1.o.a: Speed increases by 20% and time decreases by 25%
z-m-16-11.s.s1.r.a: The speed rose by 20km/h, from 80 to 100. Calculate again how many % that is using the base value (80).
z-m-16-11.s.s1.o.b: Speed increases by 25% and time also decreases by 25%
z-m-16-11.s.s1.r.b: The time dropped by 1 hour, from 5 hours to 4 hours. Calculate how many % that is with 5 hours as the base.
z-m-16-11.s.s1.o.c: Speed increases by 25% and time decreases by 20%
z-m-16-11.s.s1.r.c: You set the base values separately (80km/h, 5 hours) and calculated the ratios of change.
z-m-16-11.s.s1.o.d: There is no rule between the ratios of change of speed and time
z-m-16-11.s.s1.r.d: Compare the products of the two quantities, 80×5 and 100×4. Do you see a rule?
z-m-16-11.s.s1.explain: Speed increases by (100−80)÷80=25% and time decreases by (5−4)÷5=20%. Speed × time is a constant 400, so when the speed becomes 1.25 times, the time becomes 1÷1.25=0.8 times, that is, it decreases by 20%.
z-m-16-11.s.s2.prompt: Let y hours be the time taken to drive 400km at speed x km/h. Find and enter 3 pairs (x, y) that do not exceed the speed limit of 100km/h and arrive within 5 hours. It is accepted if the product of x and y differs from 400 by within 1 (y may be written as a decimal). Choose the speeds from different ranges among 80-84, 85-89, 90-94, 95-99, and 100.
z-m-16-11.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a speed, calculate the time taken, and check whether it is within 5 hours.
z-m-16-11.s.s2.hint.1: Find the range of speeds that satisfies both that the speed is 100km/h or less and that the time is 5 hours or less.
z-m-16-11.s.s2.ok.c1: The speed is 100km/h or less and the time is 5 hours or less.
z-m-16-11.s.s2.fail.c1: The speed must be 100km/h or less and the time must be 5 hours or less.
z-m-16-11.s.s2.ok.c2: The product of x and y agrees with 400.
z-m-16-11.s.s2.fail.c2: The product of x and y is not within 1 of 400. Calculate the time taken again.
z-m-16-11.s.s2.explain: For the time to be within 5 hours, the speed must be 80km/h or more, and because of the speed limit it must be 100km/h or less. At a speed x in between, the time is y=400÷x (hours).
z-m-16-11.s.s3.prompt: If there were no speed limit, the greater you make the speed x, the more the time taken y keeps decreasing. Even so, y cannot become 0. Write the reason using the product of x and y.
z-m-16-11.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate the time in order for speeds of 80, 100, 200, 400 and look at how the value changes.
z-m-16-11.s.s3.hint.1: Write what the value of x times y always is, and check what happens to the product if y is 0.
z-m-16-11.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the fact that 'if y is 0 the product is 0,' or the fact that the value of 'y=400÷x' is not 0? Both are valid.
z-m-16-11.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart the statement 'as the speed gets greater, the time gets closer to 0' from the statement 'it becomes 0'?
z-m-16-11.s.s3.model.0: If you multiply x and y, it is always 400. If y became 0, the product would be 0 too, and could not be 400. So however great the speed, the time cannot become 0.
z-m-16-11.s.s3.model.1: xy=400, so y=400÷x. Dividing 400 by any positive x never gives 0, so y cannot be 0. As the speed gets greater, it only gets closer to 0.
z-m-16-11.s.s3.modelNote.1: It explained with division and told apart 'getting close to 0' from 'becoming 0.'
